exercise1.prompt: Import math under the alias m and print the square root of 25

cases.name: the alias is the name the code actually uses
cases.describe: m.sqrt(25), using the alias rather than the original name

exercise1.hint: An alias replaces the name; it does not add a second one. After importing as m, the old name is no longer defined in your file.

exercise2.prompt: Import only randint from random and print a number between 1 and 100

cases.name: randint is named in the import
the import is selective, not everything at once
cases.describe: only the name you need, rather than from random import *

cases.name: randint is called with no module prefix

hiddenCases.name: prints the one number and nothing else

exercise2.hint: "Selective" is the word to hold on to. A star brings in every name the module has, including ones you never meant to use and may already have.

questions.prompt: After `import math as m`, what does `math.pi` do?
choices: Raises NameError, because math is no longer a name in this file
questions.explain: The alias is the only name bound by that import. Writing the original name afterwards asks for something that was never defined.

questions.prompt: Why is `from module import *` usually avoided?
choices: It can silently overwrite names you already defined
A reader cannot tell which module a name came from
It brings in names you never intended to use
It is slower than importing the module
questions.explain: Every objection is about clarity and collisions, not speed. The cost is that nobody reading the file can trace a name back to its module.
The selective form names the module first and the wanted names after import, separated by commas.

questions.prompt: Match each import line to what it makes available.
questions.explain: Each form binds exactly one set of names. Knowing which names you now have is the whole difference between the three.
